title: 38-60_Vermont State Employees' Association v. Vermont State Colleges
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
VERMONT STATE EMPLOYEES’
ASSOCIATION (VSEA) Docket No. 24-21,
v.
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES FACULTY
FEDERATION
(VSCFF), AFT LOCAL 3180, AFL-CIO; Docket No. 24-27,
v.
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES UNITED
PROFESSIONALS (VSCUP),
AFT VERMONT, LOCAL 6217, AFL-CIO Docket No. 24-35
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
Introduction
The Vermont State Employees’ Association, the Vermont State Colleges United
Professionals and the Vermont Colleges Faculty Federation (collectively “Unions”), representing
a total of seven bargaining units of the employees of the Vermont State Colleges (“Employer”),
each filed unfair labor practice charges alleging Vermont State Colleges violated the State
Employees Labor Relations Act when it unilaterally implemented a decision to deduct part of the
Child Care Contribution Tax (“CCC Tax”) from employees’ wages at the maximum amount
allowed by Act 76. The Unions challenge the imposition of the deduction as violative 3 V.S.A.
§961 (1) and (5).
60

The Employer disputes the charges, asserting that Act 76 imposed on it a mandate to pay
the CCC Tax and allowed it to take unilateral action regarding deductions from employee’s
wages. Because the imposition of the tax was a mandate, the tax was not the subject of
bargaining.
The parties provided stipulated facts and presented briefs to the Board Panel comprised
of David Boulanger, Acting Chair, Alan Willard, and Michelle Phelps.
STIPULATION OF FACTS
1. Vermont State Colleges (Colleges) d/b/a Vermont State University (VTSU) is an
employer under the State Employees Labor Relations Act (SELRA), 3 V.S.A. § 901, et
seq.
2. The Vermont State Colleges United Professionals (VSCUP), AFT Vermont, Local 6217,
AFL-CIO is the exclusive bargaining agent for a Professional, Administrative and
Technical (PAT) Unit (VLRB Docket No. 01-47) and a Supervisory Unit (VLRB Docket
No. 01-46). The former includes all full-time and regular part-time professional,
administrative and technical employees at the VTSU campuses, and the latter includes all
full-time and regular part-time supervisory employees at the campuses. At the time the
ULP was filed, the CBA had expired. On Monday, December 16, the successor CBA was
ratified, effective July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2028.1
3. The Vermont State Colleges Faculty Federation (VSCFF), AFT Local 3180, AFL-CIO,
is the exclusive bargaining representative of four units of employees: a) full-time faculty
1 The parties agree that the VLRB may take administrative notice of the CBAs and they may be referred to by the
parties or the VLRB in the briefs and decision.
61

and ranked librarians of VTSU (Docket No. 86-22); b) certain part-time or adjunct
faculty of VTSU, (Docket No. 91-01); c) certain part-time faculty of the Community
College of Vermont (CCV) (Docket 17-29); and d) certain part-time faculty of Northern
Vermont University Online (Docket No. 20-44). At the time the ULP was filed, the
applicable CBAs were set to expire August 31, 2024, except for CCV, which remains in
effect until August 31, 2025. On Monday, January 13, 2025, the successor CBA was
ratified for the full-time unit, effective September 1, 2024 through August 31, 2027.
4. The Vermont State Colleges Staff Federation, Vermont State Employees Association
(VSEA) is the exclusive bargaining representative all full-time, part-time, and limited
status non-faculty, non-professional and non-supervisory employees of the Vermont State
Colleges. (Docket No. 93-52). At the time the ULP was filed, the CBA expired June 30,
2024.
5. The VSCUP, VSCFF and VSEA are employee organizations under SELRA.
6. On or about June 20, 2023, Act 76 of 2023 became law in Vermont. The Act, now
codified at 32 V.S.A. §10553, requires covered employers to contribute the equivalent of
0.44 percent of each employee’s covered wages. This amount is known as Child Care
Contribution Payroll Tax. The Act further provides: “An employer may deduct and
withhold from an employee’s covered wages an amount equal to not more than one
quarter of the contribution required pursuant to subsection (b) of this section.” 32 V.S.A.
§10553(a)(1).
7. On July 1, 2024, Chief Financial and Operating Officer Sharron R. Scott notified all
Vermont-based VSC employees via email as follows:
Dear Vermont-based VSC employees,
62

In 2023, Act 76 (H.217), relating to child care and early education for
Vermonters, was passed into law. It created a Child Care Contribution (CCC)
under 32 V.S.A. Chapter 246, beginning July 1, 2024, where Vermont employers
and employees make contributions into the Child Care Contribution (CCC)
Special Fund.
The VSC recognizes the benefit of subsidizing child care for Vermonters,
including Vermont families, businesses, and communities. Effective July 1, 2024,
a 0.11% CCC Special Fund tax will be deducted from Vermont-based employees’
pay; VSC will pay the remaining 0.33% tax. The employee portion of the tax
equates to $1.10 for every $1,000 earned. For example, an employee earning
$45,000 annually will contribute $49.50 for the year; the VSC’s contribution for
this same employee will be $148.50.
For more information about Act 76 of 2023, including how it benefits you, your
family, and your community, please review the Vermont Department for Children
and Families Child Development Division’s FAQs at ACT-76-FAQs.pdf
(vermont.gov). The Let’s Grow Kids organization’s web site provides succinct
descriptions of Act 76 and its benefits: Vermont's Historic Child Care Bill —
Let's Grow Kids (letsgrowkids.org).
Our Payroll department is working with UKG, our payroll system vendor, to
implement the new tax. You will see the CCC deduction from all wages paid as
part of the first payroll in July. Should you have technical questions about how to
access your paystub, please email humanresources@vsc.edu.
Sincerely,
Sharron Scott
Sharron R. Scott
Chief Financial and Operating Officer
Vermont State Colleges
A copy of the Email is attached as Exhibit 1.
8. The Employer did not provide notice or opportunity to bargain to any union prior to such
communication or implementation.
9. As of July 1, 2024, all CBAs, except for the part-time faculty unit, the NVU online unit,
and the CCV unit, were subject to active successor contract negotiations.
63

10. The VSCUP collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) expired June 30, 2024, the VSCFF
CBAs were set to expire August 31, 2024 (except for CCV unit, which expires August
31, 2025), and the VSEA CBA expired June 30, 2024.
11. The Employer did not propose during successor contract negotiations to deduct or
withhold ¼ of the child care tax from payroll of any employee. On May 24, 2024, the
VSCFF had proposed (in bargaining for the full-time unit) that the Employer cover the
full child care tax. The VSCFF also proposed it again on June 20, 2024. On July 1, the
Employer notified the VSCFF that the implementation did not prevent the parties from
continuing to consider the VSCFF’s proposal in present bargaining.
12. The VSCUP did not make proposals regarding the child care tax, nor did it communicate
with the Employer regarding implementation.
13. On July 2, 2024, the VSEA sent a demand that the Employer cease and desist all such
deductions from employee payroll, and to communicate its intention to comply with the
law to bargaining unit employees. A copy of the email is attached as Exhibit 2.2
14. On July 3, 2024, the Employer denied the VSEA’s request and continued the deductions,
indicating that, if the VSEA desired, the parties should enter impact-bargaining A copy
of the response is attached as Exhibit 3. The VSEA declined this offer via email. A copy
of the reply email is attached as Exhibit 4.
15. That same day, the VSEA filed the instant unfair labor practice charge, #24-21, alleging
that the Employer unilaterally changed conditions of employment without providing
notice or opportunity to bargain. A copy of the charge is attached as exhibit 5.
2 The parties agree that the exhibits speak for themselves, and the stipulations merely summarize, rather than
supersede, the language contained within the exhibits.
64

16. On July 22, 2024, the VSCFF filed its unfair labor practice charge, VLRB #24-27,
asserting similar allegations as to its bargaining units. A copy of the charge is attached as
exhibit 6.
17. On July 22, 2024, the VSCUP filed its unfair labor practice charge, Docket #24-35,
asserting similar allegations as to its bargaining units. A copy of the charge is attached as
exhibit 7.
OPINION
The Unions assert the Employer violated the State Employees Labor Relations Act
(”SELRA”) by unilaterally implementing a decision to deduct part of the Child Care
Contribution Tax (“CCC” Tax) from employee wages and to deduct the maximum amount
allowed by Act 76 of 2023. The Unions argue the State was required to negotiate the amount to
be deducted from employee wages. The Employer claims that the CCC Tax under Act 76 was a
matter “prescribed and controlled by statute,” that did not impose on it a duty to negotiate the
amount to be deducted from employees’ paychecks.
The scope of issues subject to collective bargaining is broad under SELRA. See
Grievance of VSEA (re Prescription Drug Policy), 26 VLRB 305, 314 (2003). The statute
provides that “[a]ll matters relating to the relationship between the employer and employees shall
be the subject of collective bargaining except those matters which are prescribed or controlled by
statute. Such matters appropriate for collective bargaining to the extent they are not prescribed
or controlled by statute, . . . .” 3 V.S.A. § 904 (a). The Board construes narrowly exceptions to
the broad negotiation provision under SELRA, and the party asserting the exception bears the
burden of proving the exception applies. See Hackel et.al. v. VSC, 3 VLRB 175 186 (1980),
aff’d, 140 Vt. 446, 450 (1981).
65

The Employer argues that the CCC Tax under Act 76, was a matter “prescribed or
controlled by statute” and not the subject of collective bargaining under SELRA. The Employer
contends the “statute dictates how much the Colleges must contribute; the statute allows the
employer to share that burden with employees, and the statute limits how much the employer can
charge employees if it so chooses.” Employer’s Brief, at 8. The Employer also argues that even
if the Board were to find the statute does not prescribe or control the question of deductions for
employee child care contributions, the issue is not negotiable because the statute grants it the
right to charge employees a share of the tax at 0.11 percent of wages. The Employer asserts that
requiring it to negotiate this deduction strips it off this right granted by the Legislature.
Resolution of this matter requires review of the language of Act 47, to discern and give
effect to the Legislature’s intent. See IBEW Local 300 and Town of Roxbury, 30 VLRB 125,
132 (2009). Where the statute is clear and unambiguous, the Board must apply its plain and
ordinary meaning. See Grievance of Welch, 35 VLRB 19, 133 (2019).
Act 47 provides in pertinent part:
(a)(1) Each employer shall pay the Child Care Contribution on all covered wages
paid to each of the employer’s employees and shall remit those amounts to the
Department of Taxes pursuant to the provisions of this section. An employer may
deduct and withhold from an employee’s covered wages an amount equal to not
more than one quarter of the contribution required pursuant to subsection (b) of
this section. . . .
32 V.S.A. §10553
The first sentence imposes on Employer the mandatory obligation to pay the Child Care
Contribution on all covered wages. The Legislature chose the term “shall” when drafting the
first sentence, clearly expressing its intent to impose a mandate on employers to pay the CCC
Tax. The second sentence does not contain the same mandatory language. See New England
Phoenix Co., Inc. v. Grand Isle Veterinary Hosp., Inc., 2022 VT 10, ¶¶ 19-21, 216 Vt. 227, 234-
66

35 (2022) (comparing the Legislative choice of the word “shall” which the Supreme Court has
interpreted as imperative or a mandate with “may” which is permissive or discretionary).
Instead, having previously elected to impose a mandate in the first sentence, the Legislature,
chose instead to use the modal verb “may” in the second sentence, when outlining the
employer’s opportunity to deduct and withhold from employees’ wages a portion of the
contribution. Because the Legislature selected “may” in the second sentence to describe the
amounts to be deducted in contraposition to its use of the term “shall” to describe the CCC Tax
mandate, the legislative intent is clear, the deduction provision is permissive, not mandatory.
The second sentence also does not dictate the outcome of any negotiations on the subject
of employee deductions for child care contributions. The permissive language sets a cap or
ceiling on the amount of the deduction; it does not predetermine whether and what amount the
employer must deduct.
The Employer has not sustained its burden of demonstrating that Act 47 prescribes or
controls whether and what amount to deduct from employees’ wages for the child care
contribution.
The Employer has also not prevailed in its alternative argument that the child care
contribution deduction is not the subject of bargaining because the Legislature has expressly
granted this decision to the Employer. Responding to the Vermont State Colleges in similar
challenges, the Vermont Supreme Court has held that the legislative grant of authority to an
employer “does not preclude bargaining over all aspects of the power granted.” Hackel et.al v.
VSC, 140 Vt. 446, 450 ( 1981). That the Legislature has granted the Employer the right to
deduct and withhold amounts from employees to cover a portion of its CCC Tax does not render
the issue non-bargainable. See VSCFF, AFT Loc 3180, AFL-CIO v. Vermont State Colleges,
67

138 Vt. 451, 456-57 (1980) (holding that a statutory grant of authority to determine admission
and other educational standards does not render such subjects excepted from bargaining).
Nothing in Act 47 negates or undermines the express legislative intent that all matters relating to
the relationship between employers and employees are the subject of bargaining, except those
controlled or prescribed by statute. See3 V.S.A. §904(a).
The Vermont State Colleges engaged in an unfair labor practice by unilaterally deducting
one-fourth of the Child Care Contribution Tax from employees’ wages without providing notice
or an opportunity to bargain.
68

ORDER
Based on the foregoing findings of fact and for the foregoing reasons, it is hereby
ORDERED that Vermont State Colleges immediately cease and desist from deducting from
employees’ wages amounts for the Child Care Contribution Tax, reimburse or refund employees
for all such deductions, including an award of interest on deductions, and provide notice and an
opportunity to bargain.
Dated this7th day of August 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
